core: Working definition of prevention, attributed to the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021): measures that reduce the occurrence of risk factors, prevent the occurrence of disease, arrest its progress, and reduce its consequences once established
The three levels named: primary, secondary, and tertiary, each with one line and an original example (depth owned by sibling topics)
The prevention mindset: preventing a problem is usually cheaper and kinder than treating it, argued simply with an original example
Who acts: individuals, clinicians, communities, and policy, each named with one line
Prevention and risk: lowering risk factors lowers disease, with the risk topic referenced as a sibling only
The honest note: prevention is not always possible
The honest framing: prevention is the quiet work behind the loud cure
Vaccination is mentioned only as an example of primary prevention; its mechanism and programs are owned by the vaccination sibling topic
supporting: The WHO glossary's examples of screening and routine health checks as secondary prevention, corroborated by MedlinePlus's description of screening tests
CDC's statement that many chronic diseases are caused by a short list of risk behaviors, anchoring the risk-prevention connection
APHA's classic (Winslow) description of public health as prevention through organized efforts of society, organizations, communities, and individuals
outOfScope: Vaccination: mechanism, schedules, programs (sibling topic public-health:foundations:vaccination)
Risk measurement, determinants, and exposure mechanics (sibling topic public-health:foundations:risk)

claims.claim: The WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021) describes disease prevention as measures that reduce the occurrence of risk factors, prevent the occurrence of disease, arrest its progress, and reduce its consequences once established.

Primary prevention is directed at preventing the initial occurrence of a disorder, including by lowering risk factors common to many diseases such as tobacco and alcohol use, obesity, and high blood pressure.
Secondary prevention is directed at early detection of existing disease, to arrest or delay its progression and effects, for example through screening and routine health checks.
Tertiary prevention refers to disease management strategies and rehabilitation intended to avoid or reduce the risk of deterioration or complications from established disease.
Screening tests look for diseases before symptoms appear and can find diseases early, when they are easier to treat.

Many chronic diseases in the United States are caused by a short list of risk behaviors (tobacco use, poor nutrition, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol use), linking modifiable risk factors to disease occurrence.

Public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through the organized efforts and informed choices of society, organizations, public and private, communities, and individuals (Winslow, as presented by APHA).
Many of the twentieth century's great health gains, including vaccination, motor-vehicle safety, safer workplaces, and tobacco control, were prevention achievements rather than single cures.

Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, applied to the control of health problems, which is the science underneath prevention.

conflictingEvidence: Sources differ on where disease prevention ends and health promotion begins; the WHO glossary treats them as distinct but overlapping. The lesson stays with the glossary's disease-prevention definition and does not teach health promotion (a sibling topic).

'Prevention is cheaper than treatment' is a widely stated public health argument rather than a single sourced statistic. The lesson presents it as the mindset with an original example, anchoring the cost concern in CDC's statement that chronic diseases are leading drivers of U.S. health care costs, without inventing a dollar figure.

Some popular materials collapse the three levels into two (prevention and treatment) or blur secondary with tertiary. The lesson follows the canonical WHO three-level framework, with each level owned in depth by a sibling topic.
rightsIssues: The WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms 2021 is a WHO publication; its definitions are paraphrased in original prose with attribution, and no extended wording is reproduced.
The APHA page is copyrighted; only its general description of public health is restated in original prose.
The CDC pages and MedlinePlus are U.S. government works (public domain).

sourceRecords.title: About Chronic Diseases

sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-22 via Wayback Machine capture 20240508193655 of the canonical CDC URL (cdc.gov blocks direct fetch). Page last reviewed July 21, 2022. sourceRecords.title: What Is Public Health?
sourceRecords.license: Copyright APHA; facts used, no wording reproduced
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: APHA's description that public health promotes and protects the health of all people and their communities; the field aims to prevent people from getting sick or injured in the first place while health care treats people who are sick; public health focuses on entire populations while health care focuses on individual patients; examples of public health work (tracking disease outbreaks and vaccinating communities, worker safety standards, school nutrition programs, seat belt and smoke-free-air laws); the workforce includes epidemiologists, community health workers, health educators, scientists and researchers, inspectors, and public health physicians and nurses.

sourceRecords.title: Ten Great Public Health Achievements — United States, 1900-1999 (MMWR Weekly, April 2, 1999 / 48(12);241-243)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20260807162606 of the canonical CDC URL (cdc.gov blocks direct fetch). Supports: the ten great public health achievements list (vaccination; motor-vehicle safety; safer workplaces; control of infectious diseases; decline in deaths from coronary heart disease and stroke; safer and healthier foods; healthier mothers and babies; family planning; fluoridation of drinking water; recognition of tobacco use as a health hazard); vaccination resulted in eradication of smallpox and control of measles, rubella, tetanus, diphtheria, Hib, and other infectious diseases; motor-vehicle safety efforts including seat belts, child safety seats, and motorcycle helmets contributed to large reductions in motor-vehicle-related deaths; control of infectious diseases resulted from clean water and improved sanitation, dramatically reducing waterborne typhoid and cholera; since 1900 the average American lifespan lengthened by more than 30 years, about 25 years attributable to public health advances.
